summary_does_it_work: With Gemini on 50 held-out test cases, scored against the team’s hand labels: 94% decision accuracy (single-prompt baseline 84%), 93% on borderline cases (baseline 67%), 100% eligibility (baseline 68%), no invented clause IDs, 2 of its 3 wrong answers sent to a person, 90% of citations support the decision (AI-checked). About 9 seconds and 1.8 LLM calls per case.
summary_which_model: Gemini Flash-Lite is the judge. Two local 8B models (Llama 3.1, Qwen 3) on our 8 GB GPU got only 52% and 50%: they refund almost every case that should be declined. The agent beats a single prompt with every model (significantly only with Llama). OpenAI GPT-5.4 mini is the app’s paid fallback; its test run is pending (section 8.5).
timeline_outcome: Gemini: agent 94%, baseline 84% (hand labels). Llama 3.1 8B: 52% vs 30%. Qwen 3 8B: 50% vs 40%. Gemini stays the judge
design_tool_bullet: The judge can call a tool. If the retrieved clauses do not cover a gap, the judge returns search queries for search_policy as structured JSON, code runs them and the graph loops back to it (a structured-output tool call, so it works the same with every provider). With per-gap retrieval up front, no model needed it on the test set; when we removed per-gap retrieval, a planning step called the tool on its own (section 8.6). The tool is a safety net, not the main source of clauses.
model_row_gemini: Best judgement by far (94% agent accuracy); 9 s a case including free-tier pacing. The daily quota covers about one full test run
model_row_llama: Open model on our own PC, no data leaves it. 52% agent accuracy; refunds almost everything. Default local model: level with Qwen, faster, and fits fully on the 8 GB GPU
model_row_qwen: Open model on our own PC. 50% agent accuracy; refunded 22 of 23 cases that should be declined. 6.9 GB in memory, so 11% ran on the CPU
hardware: Local models ran on one desktop: Intel Core i5-13400F, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti with 8 GB of GPU memory, Windows 11, Ollama with 4-bit models. 8 GB of GPU memory limits us to models of about 8 billion parameters. We used a 10,240-token context window: it fits the largest prompt (6,800 tokens) and keeps Llama fully on the GPU (a 16k window pushed 13% onto the CPU). Larger open models would run mostly on the CPU, several times slower, and all comparison runs had to finish in one night.
how_to_read: How to read this. The agent is 10 points ahead: 7 cases only the agent got right against 2 only the baseline got right (exact McNemar p = 0.18, so not significant on 50 cases). The gain is on borderline cases (93% against 67%), where the single prompt refunds small or subjective complaints the policy does not cover, and on the rules: the baseline called 2 of the 5 ineligible cases eligible and marked 14 eligible cases ineligible. On clear cases the single prompt is slightly ahead (97% against 93%). The baseline leans towards refunding (75% of seller wins right); the agent is close to even (91% of buyer wins, 96% of seller wins). Against the brief’s targets: accuracy ≥ 80% met, eligibility 100% met (guaranteed on our data, because the cases’ order facts come from the same rules), citation ≥ 90% not yet shown (the AI check gives 90%, but no person has checked it), gain over baseline positive.
tool_use_row: Never called in the default design: per-gap retrieval already supplied the clauses (0 of 45 judged cases with Gemini, Llama and Qwen alike). Offered as an optional field in the agent-driven design it was also never used (0 of 40 Llama and 0 of 10 Gemini cases; reports/tool_field_experiment.md), so that design got its own planning step; then it is used (section 8.6)
comparison_intro: The professor asked us to try different models and explain our conclusion. We kept everything else fixed (the 50 test cases, prompts, decision guide, code, temperature 0) and changed only the model that does claim matching and judgement: Google’s gemini-flash-lite-latest in the cloud; two widely used open 8-billion-parameter models, Meta’s Llama 3.1 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3 (thinking off), running on our own PC through Ollama; and OpenAI’s gpt-5.4-mini (paid), whose runs are pending. Each ran the full agent and the single-prompt baseline. Full tables: reports/model_comparison.md.
comparison_found: Gemini is far better at the judgement; the local models get about half right. Their failure is one-sided: of the 23 eligible cases that should be declined, Gemini’s agent refunded 1, Llama’s 21 and Qwen’s 22, including change-of-mind and damage-after-delivery claims. They do not apply the policy’s exclusions, and their claim matching labels ordinary complaints as defects.
comparison_bullets: The agent beats the single prompt with every model: +10 points with Gemini, +22 with Llama, +10 with Qwen. Only Llama’s gain is statistically significant on 50 cases (17 cases only the agent got right against 6, exact McNemar p = 0.04; Gemini 7 against 2, p = 0.18). The eligibility rules in code are 100% right with every model, while the single prompt gets 68%, 86% and 90%; on clear cases Llama goes from 37% to 60%.

Citations: the agent’s final answers never cite a clause the judge was not shown, with any model. Before that check Qwen cited BPR-05, a real clause it had not been given, in 10 of 45 judged cases; the check removed it and escalated those cases. Llama’s single prompt pasted the clause heading into every citation (a real clause in the wrong format, counted separately).

Escalation: Gemini’s agent escalates 6% of cases (asking for more evidence, or low confidence) and 2 of its 3 mistakes are among them; it is right on 98% of the cases it does not escalate. Qwen’s 22% is almost entirely the BPR-05 citations (10 of 11), not low confidence; the local models never reported low confidence on their mistakes, so with them escalation only catches bad citations.

Speed: 9 s a case with Gemini (including the free tier’s pacing of at least 4.5 s between calls), 15 s with Llama, 19 s with Qwen (agent, median). Local models cost nothing per call and keep case data on the machine.

GPT-5.4 mini (OpenAI) is pending. The first 6 cases ran, at about US$0.011 a case for the agent and US$0.007 for the baseline, but the key’s organisation is on OpenAI’s free usage tier (50 requests a day per model) and the comparison needs about 500 requests. The runs resume where they stopped once the limit is lifted.
comparison_choice: Gemini Flash-Lite stays the default judge: it is by far the most accurate of the models we could test (94%, and 98% on cases it does not escalate). OpenAI GPT-5.4 mini is the app’s fallback when a Gemini call fails, capped at S$100 a month; until its test runs finish it is a backup, not a tested judge. Llama 3.1 8B is the default local model (level with Qwen, faster and fully on our GPU), as a fallback when data must stay on the machine, not a replacement: it would refund nearly every dispute, which hurts honest sellers.
comparison_hardware: 8 GB of GPU memory limited us to 8B models at 4-bit. Llama took 6.1 GB and ran fully on the GPU; Qwen took 6.9 GB and ran 11% on the CPU. 14B-and-larger models, which might close the gap, would have run mostly on the CPU, several times slower, and every run had to finish in one night. The local default was picked on the test set, so its numbers are slightly optimistic. So “cloud vs local” is also “a strong small cloud model vs 8B models at 4-bit”; the comparison cannot separate the two.
retrieval_intro: Does retrieval change the decisions, or only the citations? We ran three designs of the agent on the local models (free to run): per gap (the default), agent-driven (only general clauses up front; a planning step decides which gaps they miss and calls search_policy, then the judge decides) and none (no clauses at all). Gemini was probed on 10 cases to save the free quota.
retrieval_found: With our full decision guide, retrieval barely changes the local models’ accuracy: per gap 52% / 50%, agent-driven {la} / {qa}, none 60% / 54% (Llama / Qwen). The reason is the prompt: the decision guide restates the policy’s covered and not-covered lists, so the judge has the rules even without retrieval (tested below). Without retrieval the citations are made up: both models still cited a clause in every case, almost always BPR-02, the example ID in the prompt; the check removes them and escalates the case. In the agent-driven design Llama searched in {ls} of cases and Qwen in {qs}, at {la_calls} LLM calls a case instead of 1.8; Gemini searched only when needed (3 of 10 probe cases) and matched the per-gap design on those 10 (9 right each). So we keep per-gap retrieval as the default: as accurate, one LLM call cheaper, and predictable; the tool stays as a fallback.
risk_invented: 0% in the agent’s final answers with all three tested models. Before the check Qwen cited a clause it was not shown (BPR-05) in 22% of judged cases; the check removed it and escalated them. Gemini’s baseline 0%
risk_model: Local 8B models: 50–52% and refund nearly everything; Gemini 94%. GPT-5.4 mini not yet tested
recommendation: Recommendation to Carousell (as in the video): ready for a staff-assist pilot with Gemini as the judge, not for automatic decisions, and not with a small local model. A pilot would measure average time to resolve a dispute, the share of decisions overturned on appeal, and the share of orders using ‘Buy’.
slides_eval_row: Data; 94% vs 84% and the gain on borderline cases and the rules; the judge models (Gemini stays; local models refund almost everything)
rubric_intro: The decision guide restates the policy’s covered and not-covered lists, so the judge has the rules even without retrieval. A rubric-only guide (--guide rubric) keeps only our outcome rubric, so what is covered has to come from the retrieved clauses. Gemini was run on the first 25 test cases to save the free quota; they are all clear cases, so the borderline ones are not covered.
rubric_found: The local models cannot tell us: every 8B variant lands at 50–60% (a spread of 5 cases) and gets only 21–36% of seller wins right, whatever the prompt holds. For Gemini, retrieval can replace the restated policy (23 of 25 either way); without retrieval it declined two missing-accessory claims (G008, G043) that the policy covers, and it could cite nothing, so every case went to a person. So on this test set retrieval is not what makes the decisions accurate (Gemini mostly knows the rules). Its value is grounding every recommendation in a clause staff can check, putting coverage the model would miss in front of it, and letting a policy change be handled by re-indexing the text. A larger corpus would make retrieval matter more.
timeline_openai: Test runs stopped after 6 cases: the key’s OpenAI organisation is on the free usage tier (50 requests a day). The fallback works; its test numbers are pending
status_not_done: Not done yet: the GPT-5.4 mini test runs (blocked by the OpenAI key’s free usage tier), a person’s check of the citations, double-labelling some cases to measure agreement between labellers, and the cloud deployment.
model_row_openai: Paid; the app’s fallback when a Gemini call fails, capped at S$100 a month. Test runs pending: the key’s organisation allows 50 requests a day
gpt_row_note: Pending: stopped after 6 cases by the free usage tier (50 requests a day)
